meta.regime: The regime is still the debasement trade, but the mechanism behind it has to be restated because Friday's file had it wrong. This is not a duration rally: the 30-year US Treasury yield ROSE to 5.273% on August 21 from 5.21% a week earlier, and CNBC reports the rally from Bessent's expanded buyback programme has fizzled as investors treat the repurchases themselves - alongside the debt stock - as the risk rather than the remedy. Gold making a record 4,639 while the long bond yield rises is the signature of a fiscal-credibility trade, not falling real rates. The second leg has weakened: oil rolled over today, WTI to 85.62 and Brent to 92.98, with Iran reported to have lost significant control of the strait and Araghchi saying a deal with Oman is very close. So the dollar-negative, gold-positive core is intact and the energy-positive overlay is eroding - which is exactly why Canada comes down and Japan goes up today.

dailyRead: Start with the correction, because it changes how you hold the book. Friday's file said long US real rates were collapsing on the Treasury's doubled buyback and that this was what was driving gold and sinking the dollar. The bond market says otherwise. The 30-year US Treasury yield ROSE more than three basis points to 5.273% on Friday August 21, against 5.21% a week earlier, and CNBC's report is explicit that the rally sparked by Secretary Bessent's expanded repurchase programme has fizzled, with investor jitters about the repurchases and the debt stock hanging over the long end. Gold printing a record with the long bond yield RISING is not a duration trade at all - it is a fiscal-credibility trade, in which the intervention designed to calm the curve is itself read as the problem. Practically, that means the gold and short-dollar legs are more durable than a rate-driven story would be, because they no longer depend on yields staying down, but it also means the bond market is no longer confirming the dollar short - so treat DXY and XAU as the same trade rather than as two independent ones. Now the tape. Gold is 4,639.19, up 0.69% today, 5.05% on the week and 13.78% on the month, a record. Silver is flat at 68.88, up 4.74% on the week. Platinum is 1,892.50 and up 5.79% on the week. And crude has rolled over: WTI 85.62 and down 1.65%, Brent 92.98 and down 1.49%, with gasoline, heating oil and natural gas all down between 1.5% and 1.8% on the day. Copper fell 0.50% to 6.5467 dollars a pound as inventories eased supply concerns, and is DOWN 0.87% on the week. In FX: DXY 98.80, EUR/USD 1.16796, GBP/USD 1.36420, USD/JPY 158.985, USD/CHF 0.80134, USD/CAD 1.37592, AUD/USD 0.71714 which was Friday's biggest mover at plus 0.82%, and NZD/USD 0.59800. Note the franc: USD/CHF is 0.80134, which is back ABOVE the 0.80 handle, not below it as Friday's file claimed - the pair is testing the level, not through it. Two score changes today, both driven by hard information. JAPAN goes from 0 to +1, the second consecutive upgrade and now a positive score for the first time in this cycle. Reuters reports, on sources, that the Bank of Japan is eyeing a rate hike as soon as September and is considering hiking MORE AGGRESSIVELY than its current pace of roughly twice a year, citing price pressure from the Middle East conflict, strong global AI demand and the yen's downtrend. Polymarket assigns 84% odds to a 25 basis point increase at the September 17-18 meeting against 15% for no change - Friday's file had this at 62%, and the gap is the story. Prime Minister Takaichi, who previously called it stupid for the Bank to consider increases, is now supporting them. That sits on top of the July national CPI at 1.9% headline, 1.8% core and the highest since March, 1.9% core-core, Tokyo core 1.9%, wage growth 3.4% with real earnings positive for a sixth month, unemployment 2.5%. What still caps it at +1 rather than +2 is the external account, and here the oil rollover actually helps: a record import price index of 200, terms of trade 81.62 and a July trade balance of minus 634 billion yen all improve if Brent keeps falling. USD/JPY at 158.985 is below the 160 line the Ministry of Finance has defended, so intervention risk is low, and for the first time the rate differential is moving decisively toward the yen. CANADA goes from +1 to 0. Friday's file was explicit that oil was carrying the loonie and that the domestic side was soft. Oil is now rolling over, so the carry has gone. WTI is down 1.65% to 85.62, Iran has reportedly lost significant control of the strait, dark transits are rising and Foreign Minister Araghchi says Iran and Oman are very close to a deal on managing the waterway. Against a fading oil bid the Canadian data is genuinely poor: retail sales printed MINUS 0.8% month-on-month against plus 0.6%, the composite PMI is 49.7 and services 49.1 with both in contraction, annual GDP growth is minus 0.1% with the quarterly rate at 0.0%, the terms of trade fell to 101 and house prices are minus 2.3% year-on-year. The offsets are real - July CPI 3.0% at the ceiling of the control range with energy inflation 16.6%, producer prices plus 12.4%, employment plus 75,100 and unemployment at a two-year low of 6.4% - which is why this is a move to zero and not to negative. The practical consequence is that every CAD cross has to be re-cut: CAD/JPY flips from long to short, CAD/CHF from range to short, AUD/CAD from short to range, and EUR/CAD and GBP/CAD get more room. Europe holds +2 and stays the strongest currency on the board, but note the first genuine crack in the case. Trading Economics' ECB page now leads with the July hold and describes policymakers as having struck a more cautious, wait-and-see tone, on the grounds that softer inflation, wage growth, activity and inflation expectations have reduced the urgency for another move. Euro-area negotiated wage growth slowed to 2.44% in Q2 from 2.56%, and consumer inflation expectations fell for a third month to 2.9%. Against that, the price data is still accelerating where it matters: July HICP 2.9% with core UP to 2.5%, services 3.3%, energy HICP 10.0%, and the national prints are running hotter still with German CPI at 2.8% from 2.3%, Spain 3.6% from 3.2% and France 2.1% from 1.8%. European gas rose 6.51% on the week, UK gas 7.51% and Asian LNG 8.11%, so the energy channel Lagarde described is still open even with crude falling. Activity is improving - August composite PMI 52.1, manufacturing 52.8 and a four-year high, ZEW 31.4 - and TE's own model still has the policy rate at 2.65% refi by quarter-end, which is the September 10 hike. Depo re-verified at 2.25%. The euro is at a fourteen-week high. Keep EUR at +2 and read Thursday's meeting accounts as the test. Sterling holds +1 on the 3.75% Bank Rate, the 6-3 vote and the G10's highest gilt, with July CPI at 2.9% but core FLAT at 2.6% and services cooled to 3.4%, wages down to 4.1%. New Zealand holds +1 but with the conviction reduced. TE's model forecasts 2.75% at the September 2 meeting, which is the anchor for the score, but read the July statement carefully: the Committee said the PARTIAL REOPENING of Hormuz had lowered global oil, gas and petrochemical prices and eased near-term inflation pressure, projected headline inflation to fall from a 3.9% Q2 peak to around 2% over twelve months, and said only that further increases remain POSSIBLE with the pace data-dependent. That is a softer path than the 4.3% Q3 peak Friday's file cited, which came from the superseded May statement. Kiwi hard data is still the G10's worst - unemployment 5.6%, wage growth 2.1%, a record import bill and the largest trade gap in nearly two years, Q2 retail sales unexpectedly falling, two-year inflation expectations down to 2.34% - so treat September 2 as genuinely open rather than as a done deal. Australia holds 0 with the July labour break unrepaired - employment minus 15,827, unemployment 4.5% and a post-COVID high, participation 66.9% - but the Aussie was the strongest major on Friday at plus 0.82% and is up 7.47% year-to-date, inflation expectations rose again to 4.9% in August, and 4.35% is still the G10's highest cash rate. Copper falling back is the warning light on that: it is the cleanest leading proxy for the industrial cycle behind the Aussie, and it is down on the week even as every other metal rallied. Wednesday's July CPI indicator at 01:30Z is the resolution. Switzerland holds +1 on Q2 GDP at plus 1.5% quarter-on-quarter, a record July trade surplus of 8,141 million francs, a services PMI of 63.9 and ZEW at plus 10 from minus 25, with the policy rate pinned at 0% and TE's model flat through 2027 - and with SNB reserves having ROSEN to 768,260 million francs in July, Schlegel's repeated increased-readiness-to-intervene language is the named invalidator on every franc long. The dollar stays at -2. DXY is 98.80 and down 0.87% on the week, July payrolls were MINUS 23,000, CPI eased to 3.4% and core to 2.5%. But understand the asymmetry into Friday properly: the market is pricing roughly one-in-three odds of a September Fed HIKE, not a cut, and Warsh has no policy record, has abandoned heavy forward guidance and called his remarks a blank piece of paper. Core PCE on Wednesday is forecast to accelerate to 0.3% month-on-month while Q2 GDP is revised lower. The instruction for the week is unchanged in direction and tighter in size: run the yen, gold and franc trades, cut the oil and CAD exposure, and do not carry full risk through 14:00Z Friday.

USD.when: Sept 16-17 FOMC (hold is the base case - but ~1-in-3 is priced for a HIKE)
USD.note: Policy rate re-verified on TE this morning at 3.75% upper bound (3.50-3.75%), held on Jul 29 in a 9-3 vote with three presidents dissenting for a quarter-point hike. TE macro re-verified and unchanged: CPI 3.4% from 3.5% and a five-month low, core 2.5% from 2.6%, Q2 GDP 1.5% annualised against 2.1% with annual growth 2.1%, unemployment 4.1% from 4.2%, non-farm payrolls MINUS 23,000 from +20,000, average hourly earnings +0.1% m/m, August flash composite PMI 56.0 from 54.5 with services 56.8 and manufacturing 53.2, consumer confidence down to 51.0 from 55.2, retail sales -0.6% m/m. Two corrections matter this morning. First, the long end: the 30-year yield ROSE to 5.273% on Aug 21 from 5.21% a week earlier and CNBC reports the buyback rally has fizzled - the dollar short is no longer being confirmed by falling long yields, it is being driven by fiscal credibility, which is a different and in some ways more durable engine. Second, the direction of the risk: the market prices roughly ONE-IN-THREE odds of a September HIKE, not a cut, so a hawkish Warsh is the consensus tail rather than a surprise. The week's structure: Wednesday Aug 26 at 12:30Z brings core PCE, forecast to ACCELERATE to 0.3% m/m, alongside a Q2 GDP second estimate expected LOWER - a hot-inflation, slowing-growth pairing that is awkward for a committee with three hawkish dissenters on record. Then Friday Aug 28 at 14:00Z Kevin Warsh delivers his first Jackson Hole keynote as Chair, expected around 10:00 ET, with the Kansas City Fed confirming the agenda Wednesday evening. He has moved away from heavy forward guidance, told reporters the remarks would address long-term structural questions, and described the speech as 'a blank piece of paper right now'; roughly 69% of surveyed fund managers expect a neutral tone. Hold the short at -2 through Wednesday and carry reduced size through Friday.

EUR.when: Sept 10, 12:15Z (TE model still 2.65% refi by quarter-end - but the page now says 'wait-and-see')
EUR.note: Deposit facility re-verified on TE at 2.25% after the Jun 11 hike, with main refinancing at 2.40% and marginal lending at 2.65%. Use the 2.25% depo, never the 2.40% headline. Honest change of emphasis today: TE's ECB summary now leads with the July 23 hold and says policymakers have struck a more CAUTIOUS, wait-and-see tone because softer inflation, wage growth, activity and inflation expectations have reduced the urgency for another move. The supporting evidence for that dovish read is real - euro-area negotiated wage growth slowed to 2.44% in Q2 from 2.56%, consumer inflation expectations fell for a third month to 2.9% from 3.0%, producer prices decelerated to 4.6% y/y, food inflation is only 0.8% and retail sales -0.3% m/m. But the price data that actually decides September is still accelerating: July HICP 2.9% from 2.8% with core UP to 2.5% from 2.4%, services 3.3% from 3.2%, energy HICP 10.0% from 8.5%, and the national prints hotter again with Germany 2.8% from 2.3%, Spain 3.6% from 3.2%, France 2.1% from 1.8% and Italy 2.9%. The energy channel Lagarde named is still open even with crude falling, because European gas rose 6.51% on the week, UK gas 7.51%, German gas 7.23% and Asian LNG 8.11%. Activity is improving: Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q and +1.0% y/y, August composite PMI 52.1 and a nine-month high, manufacturing 52.8 and a four-year high, services 51.7, ZEW 31.4 from 23.4, consumer confidence -15.5, unemployment stable at 6.3%. TE's own model still puts the policy rate at 2.65% by the end of this quarter, which is the September 10 move. EUR holds +2. The July meeting accounts land Thursday Aug 27 at 09:30Z and are the cleanest test of whether the wait-and-see language is tone or substance. EUR/USD 1.16796, a fourteen-week high.

GBP.when: Sept 17 (Jul 30 = 6-3 hold; the hawkish evidence keeps thinning)
GBP.note: Bank Rate re-verified on TE at 3.75%, held Jul 30 but 6-3 with a third member joining the dissent against a 7-2 consensus. Both decisive prints have landed and both cut the same way once you look past the headline. Labour: wage growth eased to 4.1% including bonuses from 4.4%, employment change fell to +83,000 from +147,000, unemployment held at 4.9% against expectations of a fall to 4.8%, and the claimant count FELL 11,000. Prices: July CPI rose to 2.9% from 2.6%, the first increase in the annual rate since March, but the driver was administered energy on the Ofgem cap adjustment - core CPI held FLAT at 2.6% and services inflation COOLED to 3.4% from 3.6%. Activity is decent but decelerating: Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q against +0.6%, annual rate up to 1.2%, August composite PMI 52.5. The 10-year gilt near 5.1% is still the G10's highest and is doing more for sterling than the MPC is; UK electricity is +4.29% on the week and UK gas +7.51%, which points at another administered-energy uplift in October. GBP holds +1. With services inflation falling and wages easing the three dissenters are running out of evidence, so express sterling against the dollar, the Aussie and the Canadian dollar rather than against the euro, the franc or - now - the yen. Cable 1.36420.

JPY.when: Sept 18 (84% priced on Polymarket - and Reuters says the BoJ wants a FASTER pace)
JPY.note: Policy rate re-verified on TE at 1.00%, held Jul 31 in an 8-1 vote with Takata dissenting for 1.25%. UPGRADE from 0 to +1 - the first positive yen score of this cycle. The new information is the pricing and the guidance, not the data. Reuters reports on sources that the Bank of Japan is eyeing a rate hike as soon as September AND is considering hiking more aggressively than its current pace of roughly twice a year, citing price pressure from the Middle East conflict, strong global AI demand and the yen's downtrend. Polymarket assigns 84% to a 25bp increase at the September 17-18 meeting against 15% for no change; Friday's file carried 62%. Prime Minister Takaichi, who once called it stupid for the Bank to consider increases, now supports them. The data underneath is already there: July national CPI 1.9% from 1.6% and the highest since December 2025, core 1.8% from 1.6% and the highest since March, core-core 1.9% from 1.7%, Tokyo core 1.9% and Tokyo headline 2.0%, services 1.2%, goods 2.7%, food 3.5%, PPI 7.2%, inflation expectations 2.7%. The domestic case is the best in three decades: June labour cash earnings +3.4% y/y, real earnings +1.6% and positive for a sixth month, unemployment 2.5%, jobs-to-applications 1.18, industrial output +4.9% y/y, machinery orders +16.9% y/y, August Reuters Tankan 18 from 13, manufacturing PMI 55.1 and services 52.3. The external account is still the cap - a RECORD import price index of 200, import prices +29.1% y/y, terms of trade 81.62 and a July trade balance of MINUS JPY 634bn - but note that today's oil rollover works in the yen's favour on every one of those lines, which is why the upgrade and the crude downgrade belong in the same file. USD/JPY 158.985 is clear of the 160 line where the MoF has already acted. Tokyo August CPI and July unemployment land Thursday Aug 27 at 23:30Z and are now a genuine high-impact event.

AUD.when: Sept 29 (hold - and Wednesday's July CPI indicator is the resolution)
AUD.note: Cash rate re-verified on TE at 4.35%, held unanimously on Aug 11 with Governor Bullock revealing the Board did NOT discuss a cut - only whether to raise or hold. The July labour force survey damaged that frame and has not repaired it: employment FELL 15,827 against consensus of +20-25k, full-time rose 16,333 but part-time collapsed 32,160, unemployment rose to 4.5% and the post-COVID high, participation fell to 66.9% and the employment-to-population ratio to 63.9%, job vacancies fell to 330,000, terms of trade dropped to 112 from 117, business confidence is -6 and the current account deficit a record -AUD 27.1bn. What keeps AUD at 0 rather than negative is price and carry: 4.35% is the G10's highest, Q2 weighted median CPI ROSE to 3.7% from 3.5%, trimmed mean 3.6%, services 4.0%, headline 3.8%, and consumer inflation expectations rose AGAIN to 4.9% in August from 4.7%. Consumer confidence jumped to 88.9 and August PMIs are expansionary at 52.5 composite. Market-wise the Aussie was the strongest major on Friday at +0.82% to 0.71714 and is +7.47% year-to-date. The warning light is copper: at 6.5467 USD/lb it fell 0.50% today on easing inventories and is DOWN 0.87% on the week while gold, silver and platinum all rallied - copper is the cleanest leading proxy for the industrial cycle behind the Aussie, so a copper breakdown is the early signal on every AUD long. RBA Minutes land Tuesday Aug 25 at 01:30Z and the July CPI indicator Wednesday Aug 26 at 01:30Z; the CPI is the one that matters.

NZD.when: Sept 2, 02:00Z (TE model 2.75% - but treat it as genuinely open, not a done deal)
NZD.note: OCR re-verified on TE at 2.50% after the 25bp hike on Jul 8, the first in three years. NZD holds +1 but with the conviction cut, and this is a correction to Friday's framing. TE's model does forecast 2.75% for September 2, which is what anchors the score. But the July statement itself is softer than Friday's file implied: the Committee said the PARTIAL REOPENING of the Strait of Hormuz has lowered global oil, gas and petrochemical prices and eased near-term inflation pressures, projected headline inflation to decline from a peak of 3.9% in Q2 2026 to around 2% over the next twelve months, noted the economy LOST momentum in the June quarter, and said only that further increases remain POSSIBLE with the pace dependent on incoming data. The 4.3% Q3 peak Friday's file quoted came from the superseded May statement. Governor Breman's 'sooner and more sharply than indicated' line is from a speech on May 29, not from July, so it should not be treated as current guidance. The survey side is genuinely better - business confidence 56.1 from 36.6, ANZ Roy Morgan consumer confidence 99.3 from 91.3, GDT +2.3% - and Q2 CPI at 4.1% with core 3.2% is above the band. But the hard data is the G10's weakest and got worse: unemployment 5.6% and the highest since Q3 2015, wage growth only 2.1%, youth unemployment 17.2%, Q2 retail sales unexpectedly FELL, imports hit a record high and the trade gap is the largest in nearly two years, the manufacturing PMI fell to 54.3 and services 50.6, private sector growth eased. Two-year business inflation expectations fell to 2.34% from 2.53%, the lowest since Q4 2025. NZD/USD 0.59800, +1.49% on the week and near multi-month highs. Trade the kiwi long against the dollar and the Aussie, keep it small against the other +1 currencies, and treat September 2 as a real two-way event.

CAD.when: Sept 2, 13:45Z (hold - and with oil rolling over there is nothing else holding CAD up)
CAD.note: Policy rate re-verified on TE at 2.25%, held Jul 15 for a sixth straight meeting. DOWNGRADE from +1 to 0. The logic is the one Friday's file set out: oil was carrying the loonie and the domestic side was soft. Oil has now rolled over - WTI 85.62 and down 1.65% today, Brent 92.98 and down 1.49% - and the geopolitical premium behind it is eroding, with CNN reporting Iran has lost significant control of the strait and Araghchi saying a deal with Oman is very close. Strip the crude bid out and the Canadian data does not support a positive score: retail sales printed MINUS 0.8% m/m against +0.6%, the composite PMI is 49.7 and services 49.1 with both in CONTRACTION, annual GDP growth is -0.1% with the quarterly rate at 0.0%, the terms of trade fell to 101 from 107 despite the oil move, business confidence slipped to 55.1 and house prices are -2.3% y/y. catalysts.event: Strait of Hormuz / Iran-US de-escalation watch
catalysts.note: The direction has changed: CNN reports Iran has LOST significant control of the strait, dark transits rose 27%, and Araghchi says an Oman deal is 'very close' - though Iran still ties reopening to reparations and sanctions relief. Drives USOIL, CAD, JPY and the haven complex at once.

Reserves ROSE to CHF 768,260m in July from 758,851m and Schlegel keeps reaffirming increased readiness to intervene against rapid or one-way franc appreciation. The named invalidator on every CHF long.

USD/JPY at 158.985 is clear of the 160 line where the Ministry has already acted, so risk is low. A hawkish Warsh that pushes the pair back toward 160 puts it live again - and would fight the BoJ's own tightening.

geopolitics: The direction of the Iran-US story changed this week, and it changed against the oil trade. The naval blockade is still in force, barring ships to and from any Iranian port, and Iran's official position is unmoved: Tehran ties any reopening of the Strait of Hormuz to US concessions including war reparations and the lifting of sanctions, and an Iranian military leader vowed over the weekend that Tehran 'will not submit'. The UAE Foreign Ministry has accused the IRGC of piracy and of using the strait as a tool of economic coercion, and three ADNOC vessels have been hit by missiles and drones this month. But the flow data and the diplomacy are both moving the other way. CNN reported on August 18 that Iran has LOST significant control of the strait: roughly 130 ships a day are now transiting, dark transits in which chartered tankers switch off transponders and offload in the Gulf of Oman have risen about 27% over the past week, and product tankers are the most common vessel type getting through. Foreign Minister Araghchi says Iran and Oman are 'very close' to a deal on managing the waterway, and Oman's Foreign Ministry describes those talks as positive and constructive - while cautioning that continued attacks on vessels put progress at risk. Tehran maintains that the Oman track is separate from reopening the strait, which is exactly the ambiguity the market is now pricing. The FX transmission has therefore flipped sign on two of its four legs. Crude fell today, WTI to 85.62 and Brent to 92.98, which is why CANADA comes down to 0 - the loonie's oil leg was its only support against retail sales at -0.8% and both PMIs below 50 - and why JAPAN's upgrade is more robust than it looks, because a falling oil price directly repairs a record import price index of 200, terms of trade of 81.62 and a July trade deficit of 634 billion yen. The two legs that have not flipped are European gas, which rose 6.51% on the week with UK gas up 7.51% and Asian LNG up 8.11% and keeps the ECB's energy channel open even as crude falls, and the haven complex, where gold made a record 4,639 and the franc is testing 0.80 against the dollar. Trade it as a slowly de-escalating condition with fat tails: the Muscat channel is the route to a genuine unwind of the crude premium, and for the first time this year the flow data is pointing that way - but a single vessel attack reverses it inside a session.
